newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Izetbegovic - symbol of Bosnia's struggle.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic - symbol of Bosnia's struggle.

text.p: Alija Izetbegovic, who on Wednesday won the contest to lead Bosnia's new three-man presidency, is the country's most prominent Moslem leader.
More than any other man, the austere 70-year-old president came to symbolise the Bosnian government's defiance through more than three years of war .
Lionised by supporters, demonised by opponents, Izetbegovic stayed in Sarajevo throughout its long siege by Bosnian Serbs and suffered alongside his people.

From his sand-bagged presidency in the capital he chastised an increasingly embarrassed world for failing to help his state defend itself against the Serbs, gradually turning battlefield defeats into diplomatic gains.

Critics say he is a Moslem fundamentalist at heart and accuse him of growing intolerance, using the machinery of his Moslem nationalist Party of Democratic Action (SDA) to intimidate and harrass opponents.
Loyalists say he is the father of the nation whose obduracy in the face of overwhelming odds allowed his country to survive.
During the election campaign, he studiously avoided the nationalist rhetoric of some SDA leaders and spoke the language of reconciliation.
But critics say his advocacy of the single, unified Bosnia of the Dayton peace agreement appears to stem more from territorial ambition than real commitment to multi-ethnicity.
Izetbegovic, born in 1925 in Bosanski Samac, has spent his entire life in Sarajevo except for serving two terms, totalling nine years, as a political prisoner in the former Yugoslavia.
He was elected to Bosnia's pre-war collective presidency in 1990, when the country was part of Yugoslavia.
Izetbegovic declared independence for his country in April 1992 -- precipitating the 43-month war with Serb and Croats separatists who feared Moslem domination.
The United Nations and Western powers recognised Bosnian independence when the war began, but their support was half-hearted and fed suspicions of pro-Serb sympathies.
Izetbegovic, a lawyer by training, was accused of naivety and inexperience. But as the war progressed, he grew in stature.
With the international community maintaining an arms embargo, freezing the military advantage of the Belgrade-assisted Serbs, he refused to flinch.

International outrage against the Serbs finally prompted NATO air strikes against them. At the same time an uneasy Moslem-Croat alliance delivered battlefield victories and brought the Serbs to the negotiating table.
Unlike Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, Izetbegovic was never a communist. Instead, Islamic activism has been the motor of his career.
It earned him a jail term of three years in 1946 and another of 14 years -- of which he served five -- in the 1980s.

The latter followed Izetbegovic's publication of an "Islamic Declaration" which has been used by his Serb opponents to buttress their claim their claim that the Moslems' aim is to set up a fundamentalist state on Western Europe's doorstep.
